title: How Does a USB Stick Remember Your Files With No Power?
sources: TechTarget 'floating gate transistor (FGT)': the oxide layer that surrounds the floating gate keeps the electrons trapped, whether or not the flash device has power; when electrons are present on the floating gate, current can't flow through the transistor and the bit state is 0

Wikipedia 'Flash memory': each cell is a floating-gate transistor insulated by an oxide layer; electrons are moved onto the floating gate through the insulating layer (hot-electron injection / Fowler-Nordheim tunneling); default/erased cell = 1, programmed = 0; read by checking whether current flows; NAND can only be erased in whole blocks

Wikipedia 'Flash memory': Fujio Masuoka invented flash memory at Toshiba in 1980; the name 'flash' was suggested by his colleague Shoji Ariizumi because the erasure process reminded him of the flash of a camera
PetaPixel 'Did You Know: Flash Memory is Named After the Camera Flash' (2017): Ariizumi was reminded of a camera flash; the name highlights the fast way flash memory can erase data

lines.text: How does a USB stick remember your files with no power?
lines.caps: HOW DOES A *USB | STICK *REMEMBER | YOUR *FILES | WITH NO *POWER?

lines.text: Inside are billions of tiny cells, each holding one bit.
lines.caps: INSIDE ARE *BILLIONS | OF TINY *CELLS | *EACH HOLDING | ONE *BIT

lines.text: Every cell has a little box called a floating gate,
lines.caps: EVERY *CELL HAS | A LITTLE *BOX | CALLED A *FLOATING | *GATE

lines.text: sealed in a thin wall of insulation.
When you save, a voltage shoves electrons through that wall,
lines.caps: WHEN YOU *SAVE | A *VOLTAGE | *SHOVES ELECTRONS | THROUGH THAT *WALL

lines.text: A full box blocks the current, that's a zero,
lines.caps: A *FULL BOX | *BLOCKS THE CURRENT | THAT'S A *ZERO

lines.text: an empty one lets it flow, that's a one.
lines.caps: AN *EMPTY ONE | LETS IT *FLOW | THAT'S A *ONE

lines.text: Unplug it, and the electrons just stay trapped,
so your files are still there next time.
And erasing wipes a whole block in one go,
which reminded a Toshiba engineer of a camera flash,
so that's why it's called flash memory.
They're locked in a tiny jail.
